solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Broken patterns in cathedral wing

indicators.note: something broken is no longer in its original form, so these letters must be put back together differently

blocks.note: taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: Damaged decorative designs in part of a cathedral, perhaps on tiles or stained glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A transept is either arm of a cross-shaped church, crossing the nave at right angles.

clue.text: Capture bear

blocks.note: first meaning: to seize, as in taking a town
second meaning: to endure, as in 'I can't stand it'

explanation.walkthrough: 'bear' looks like the animal being caught, but it is the verb meaning tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb can mean to seize something by force and also to put up with or tolerate something.

clue.text: Tumbler's performance involving wild boar

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so these letters run loose into a new order
involving means including within, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: an act is a performance on stage
taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: A circus tumbler's routine features an untamed wild pig.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbler is a gymnast performing somersaults and handsprings, the same as an acrobat.

clue.text: Economy by good people shows redeeming quality

blocks.note: a saving is an economy made
G is the abbreviation for good
a race is a people or nation

explanation.surface: Thrift practised by decent folk is a virtue that compensates for their faults.
explanation.definitionFit: A saving grace is the one good feature that makes up for someone's or something's shortcomings.

clue.text: Dad holding a fork out for fruit

indicators.note: holding means gripping on the inside, so what follows sits within the first piece

blocks.note: an everyday word for father
taken as written
to fork out is to pay up

explanation.surface: A father with a fork in hand, ready to spend money on fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a fork' looks like cutlery, but the A stands alone and 'fork out' is the phrasal verb meaning spend.
explanation.definitionFit: Papaya is a tropical fruit with orange flesh, also called pawpaw.

clue.text: Obscene Oxbridge sportsperson

blocks.note: first meaning: smutty, as in a risqué film or joke
second meaning: someone who has represented Oxford or Cambridge University in a sport

explanation.walkthrough: Oxford and Cambridge award a 'Blue' to students who compete for the university against the other, named after the colours of the two teams.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means indecent in slang and also names a varsity athlete honoured with university colours.

clue.text: Number close enough?

blocks.note: first meaning: something that numbs
second meaning: nearby, in the neighbourhood

explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' reads as a figure, but it is numb-er, something that deadens feeling; a local is an anaesthetic given to one area.
explanation.definitionFit: A local anaesthetic numbs part of the body, and the adjective describes something situated nearby.

clue.text: Drunken ordeal and party in fabulous place

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of order, so these letters lurch into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, as the fodder
a do is a party or social event

explanation.surface: A boozy trial and a celebration in some marvellous location.
explanation.definitionFit: El Dorado is the legendary city of gold sought by Spanish explorers, a mythical land of riches.

clue.text: Knock-out verse about Irish city

indicators.note: going about something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: the standard boxing abbreviation
V is the abbreviation for verse
IR is the abbreviation for Irish

explanation.surface: A devastating poem written about a city in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irish city' looks like the definition, but Irish is just the abbreviation and the city is Russian; the abbreviation sits after the first letter of the boxing term.
explanation.definitionFit: Kirov is a Russian city on the Vyatka river, named after the Soviet politician Sergei Kirov.

clue.text: Cop lied — somehow did his job?

indicators.note: somehow says the letters come together by some unspecified method, so they need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: A police officer told a lie; was he really doing his work?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a comment on the officer, and the anagram's answer is exactly what a cop does.
explanation.definitionFit: Policing is a cop's work, so the past tense describes him carrying out his duty.

clue.text: Lumbermen accepting fine: DA to direct piercing glare

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the following pieces go inside the first

blocks.note: loggers fell trees for timber
OK means all right
taken as written

explanation.surface: Timber workers paying a penalty while a District Attorney glares at them.
explanation.definitionFit: To look daggers is an idiom for staring at someone with intense hostility.

clue.text: Vengeful cook spreading only brie on roll

indicators.note: spreading something out disturbs its shape, so these letters are laid out in a new order
placed on something means sitting after it, so the roll comes first and the spread follows it

blocks.note: a bun is a bread roll
taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: A cook taking revenge by spreading nothing but brie on a bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the film Fatal Attraction, in which a spurned lover boils her ex's pet rabbit.
explanation.definitionFit: A bunny boiler is a slang term for an obsessive, revenge-seeking former lover, and the film's one literally cooked a pet.

clue.text: Book kept in PO Box for corporation

indicators.note: something kept in a place is held inside it, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: taken as written
the box is British slang for the television, the telly
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A book stored in a Post Office box on behalf of a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PO Box' looks like one unit, but PO is taken as written and Box means TV. Corporation is old British slang for a large belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is a jocular old word for a paunch, which is the same thing as a potbelly.

clue.text: Unpopular time for power cut

blocks.note: out of favour, no longer in fashion
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A deeply unpopular moment to have the electricity go off.
explanation.definitionFit: An outage is a period when a supply such as electricity is interrupted.

clue.text: Plantagenet king inside unleashed war dogs

indicators.note: inside says the letters sit within the words that follow, spanning their boundaries

blocks.note: the run of letters across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A medieval king lets loose the dogs of war, echoing Shakespeare's 'Cry havoc'.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward I, II and III were kings of the Plantagenet dynasty that ruled England from 1154 to 1485.

clue.text: Roman commander having a vice we hear?

indicators.note: we hear says the word is identified by its sound when spoken rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a vice is a tool that grips, a gripper

explanation.surface: A Roman general with some bad habit, or so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vice' wants to be a moral failing; it is the workshop clamp.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Agrippa was the Roman general who won the battle of Actium for Augustus.

clue.text: Street philosopher one unlikely to give up

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
A. J. Ayer was a British philosopher

explanation.surface: A street-corner thinker who never abandons an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: A stayer is a horse or person with stamina who keeps going to the end.

clue.text: Ferocious creature let in — beggar devoured

indicators.note: food that has been devoured is broken up and mangled, so these letters are churned into another order

blocks.note: taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: A wild animal is admitted and a vagrant gets eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bengal tiger, native to the Indian subcontinent, is a large and dangerous big cat.

clue.text: Beat up a Liberal in old province

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician attacked in a former province.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat up' reads as assault, but 'up' is the reversal signal for a word meaning beat.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a province of South Africa until 1994, now part of KwaZulu-Natal.

clue.text: Line dropped from fashion — problem for looker?

indicators.note: something dropped from a group is left out, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line
style means fashion

explanation.surface: A clothing line is cut from the fashion range, a blow for a model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looker' suggests a beautiful model, but it is anyone who looks, i.e. with an eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, a nuisance for the eye.

clue.text: Aquatic mammal seen in play regularly — big draw?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
something seen in a place sits within it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: an otter is a river-dwelling mammal
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: An otter turns up in a theatre production, perhaps as a star attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big draw' plays on draw as a crowd-puller, but a lottery is literally decided by a draw.
explanation.definitionFit: A lottery is a game of chance settled by drawing numbers, and a large one counts as a major prize draw.

clue.text: One making new life abroad — former postman?

blocks.note: ex- means formerly
Postman Pat is the title character of a British children's TV series

explanation.surface: Someone emigrating who might once have delivered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An expat, short for expatriate, is a person living outside their native country.

clue.text: Not the white team according to report

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is identified by how it sounds when spoken

blocks.note: a yoke is a pair of oxen harnessed together, a team

explanation.surface: A sports report on a side that does not play in white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White' suggests a team's kit, but it is the white of an egg.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg has a white and a yellow centre, so the part that is not the white is the yolk.

clue.text: Fastest guns to win this international competition?

definitions.text: Fastest guns to win this international competition?

blocks.clueFragment: Fastest guns to win this international competition?
blocks.note: surface reading: quick-draw marksmen competing in a shooting tournament between countries

blocks.clueFragment: Fastest guns to win this international competition?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the nations that build weapons quickest prevail in a military build-up between rivals

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fastest guns' evokes Wild West gunslingers, but here it means the countries that produce weaponry most quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names rivalry between nations to amass more and better military weapons, as in the Cold War.
